questions.prompt: Von Behring transferred blood from an immune guinea pig to another, which became immune. What did this show?

options.text: Immunity to diphtheria is inherited from the parents
A factor in the blood (antibodies) carried the immunity
Guinea pigs have no immune system of their own
Diphtheria toxin is harmless to most guinea pigs

questions.prompt: Why did the second guinea pig's immunity last only about three weeks?

options.text: It received preformed antibodies that broke down
Guinea pigs are unable to make any antibodies
The diphtheria toxin mutated into a new form
Its own memory cells died off after three weeks

questions.explanation: Antibodies have a ~3-week half-life; no memory cells were made.

questions.prompt: Which part of an antibody determines its class (IgG, IgM, etc.)?
questions.explanation: Immune cells have receptors for the constant region.

questions.prompt: An antibody binds only one specific antigen because of the shape of its:
questions.explanation: Variable regions form a lock-and-key binding site.

questions.prompt: Which statement about antibody mechanisms is FALSE?

options.text: Neutralization works by bursting bacteria with pores.
Antivenom works by neutralizing a toxin.

questions.explanation: Neutralization blocks attachment; pores come from complement's MAC.

questions.prompt: Antibody-dependent cytotoxicity is especially useful against:

options.text: Large eukaryotic invaders like parasitic worms
Free-floating LPS released by dead bacteria
Toxins dissolved in the blood plasma
Viruses before they attach to host cells

questions.explanation: Eosinophils or NK cells destroy antibody-coated large cells.

questions.prompt: Which antibody is a pentamer and the first made after exposure?
questions.explanation: Its monomer form also serves as the B cell receptor.
Natural passive immunity for the fetus.

questions.prompt: Which antibody is a dimer found in breast milk, saliva, and mucus?
A person with hay fever has an overreaction involving mast cells. Which antibody is responsible?
questions.explanation: Mast cells have IgE-specific receptors; allergies are hypersensitivities.

questions.prompt: Explain clonal selection, including what selects the B cell and the two kinds of cells produced.
questions.explanation: Bone-marrow stem cells make billions of B cells, each with a unique B cell receptor. An antigen binds the B cell whose receptor fits, selecting it. It clones itself into plasma cells (secrete large amounts of matching antibody) and memory B cells (keep receptors and remain in circulation for a faster secondary response).

questions.prompt: Why don't plasma cells need B cell receptors?

options.text: They only make IgE, which already sits on mast cells
They live in mucus, where receptors would be destroyed
They are actually T cells, which use T cell receptors
They don't recognize antigens — they just secrete antibodies

questions.explanation: Memory cells keep receptors; plasma cells don't.

questions.prompt: On a titer graph, which feature shows a secondary response?

options.text: A fast, much higher, longer-lasting IgG rise
Lower IgG than the primary response
A week-long lag before any antibody appears

questions.explanation: Memory cells make the response fast and strong.

questions.prompt: A baby receives antibodies through breast milk. This is:
questions.explanation: Preformed antibodies from mother, by a natural route.

questions.prompt: A snakebite victim gets antivenom. This is:
questions.explanation: Injected preformed antibodies act immediately but don't create memory.

questions.prompt: Compare active and passive immunity in terms of whose B cells are involved, speed, and how long it lasts.
questions.explanation: Active: your own B cells are selected and make plasma and memory cells — slower to develop but long-lasting. Passive: you receive preformed antibodies — immediate protection but temporary (antibody half-life ~3 weeks), with no memory cells.
